hero.body:
Homeowners across Florida are discovering that insurance companies are using credit reports and data profiles to set their premiums, adding a new factor to the state's ongoing insurance crisis. Todd, a Palm Beach County homeowner, contacted WPTV after his insurer raised his premium based on a LexisNexis rating in his credit report. The practice affects policyholders statewide who are already grappling with rising costs for impact windows and roof replacements.

Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said insurance companies use detailed credit and data reports to assess the risk of each policyholder and set rates either higher or lower. The data companies, including credit bureaus, now compile extensive information on consumers beyond traditional credit scores. Norberg explained that insurers can pull credit scores specifically tailored for different types of underwriting, whether for auto or property insurance, and these reports contain far more information than they used to.

The issue first came to light in July when a Delray Beach driver showed WPTV how a lengthy credit and data report was affecting a premium quote. The reports pull from multiple sources to create risk profiles that insurers use to price policies. Different insurance companies interpret the data in these reports differently, but most use them to evaluate policyholder risk across their Florida books of business.

Many Florida homeowners remain unaware that their credit information is being factored into their insurance costs. The practice adds another layer of complexity to a market where homeowners are already facing premium increases and coverage challenges. Norberg noted that the scope of data collection has expanded significantly, giving insurers access to a broader range of information about policyholders than in previous years. WPTV reported it plans to investigate the practice further as more homeowners express concern about how these reports affect their insurance costs.
hero.headline: Florida homeowners learn credit reports now drive insurance premiums statewide

hero.angle: Lead with the local case of PSL High football player Emmanuel Nelson, detained by ICE after a school-zone speeding stop, and the community/team fallout as he awaits removal proceedings.

hero.body:
Port St. Lucie High School senior Emmanuel Nelson, an 18-year-old football player, has been held in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody since late August after a traffic stop for speeding through a school zone put him on federal immigration enforcement's radar. Nelson was stopped on Southeast Lennard Road near Southeast Grand Drive and Southeast Union Park Drive on the morning of August 19 after Deputy Daigneault clocked him driving 45 miles per hour in a 20-mile-per-hour school zone. He was cited for unlawful speed in a school zone, a civil infraction that does not require a court appearance.

 ICE arrested Nelson on August 22, three days after the traffic citation, during what the agency called an enforcement operation before transferring him to ICE custody. In a statement, an ICE spokesman described Nelson as an immigrant from Haiti living in the country illegally. ICE said Nelson entered the United States legally on January 16, 2016, but later violated the terms of his admission. He remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

 On the football field, Nelson is a rising senior on the Port St. Lucie High School defense, according to comments head coach Everette Alford made in May. Nelson played in the August 14 Kickoff Classic against Fort Pierce Central High School, five days before he was cited and taken into custody.

 ICE's statement also pointed to the agency's push for self deportation, telling immigrants in the country illegally that the government is offering money and a flight home through its CBP Home app, and warning of arrest and removal for those who do not take the offer.

cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening, but by that point the Port St. Lucie tornado had already dissipated. The EF-0 tornado featured very shallow circulation and was not picked up well by radar, leaving reports of the funnel cloud as the trigger for the warning. The tornado became a waterspout at one point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said the event was unique because it was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not typical during summer months. The tornado was generated by a typical summer afternoon thunderstorm and had winds of 60 to 70 mph. Ulrich said the event serves as a reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

The National Weather Service issues tornado warnings once it is able to detect a tornado. The agency recommends having multiple ways to receive warnings to keep residents and their loved ones safe.
cards.headline: National Weather Service explains why Port St. Lucie tornado warning came after EF-0 twister had dissipated
cards.teaser: The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning for Port St. Lucie on Sunday evening after the EF-0 tornado had already dissipated. The shallow circulation made it difficult for radar to detect the tornado, which was confirmed only after funnel cloud reports came in.

cards.body:
Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement. The decision follows the City Commission's choice not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month.

Commissioner Michael Broderick voted against the appointment, arguing the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island, including potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. He said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island.

Supporters said Wallace's previous experience in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager makes her well-positioned to step into the role and help keep city business moving. The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney, authorizing up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process.
cards.headline: Fort Pierce debates interim city attorney appointment amid development decisions
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while searching for a permanent replacement, sparking debate over upcoming development decisions.

cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening. At the point in which the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. Because this tornado featured very shallow circulation, it was not picked up well by the radar. Reports of the funnel cloud are what then prompted the warning of the EF-0 tornado that became a waterspout at a point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said what made Sunday's event unique was that it was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not something typically seen during the summer months. The tornado was one of the typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado that had winds of 60 to 70 miles per hour. Ulrich called it a good reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

The National Weather Service is in charge of issuing tornado warnings. Once the National Weather Service is able to detect a tornado, it will always issue a tornado warning. The agency says residents should make sure they have multiple ways to receive these warnings to keep themselves and their loved ones safe.
cards.headline: National Weather Service explains tornado warning issued after Port St. Lucie twister
cards.teaser: The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds came in Sunday evening, though the EF-0 tornado had already dissipated when the warning was issued.

cards.body:
Fort Pierce's legal department is losing three attorneys as the city prepares to handle several significant development decisions, including proposals on South Hutchinson Island. The City Commission chose not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin will leave at the end of the month. Commissioner Michael Broderick said the departures leave Fort Pierce without independent legal representation to address volatile projects expected before the commission soon.

Broderick pointed to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island, including potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. He said removing those restrictions could allow much taller development on the island. Broderick told CBS12 News that several volatile projects are slated to come before the City Commission in short order.

Commissioners voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while conducting a search for a permanent replacement. Broderick voted against the appointment and said the city appointed the assistant city manager to be a charter officer, which he believes reeks of duplicity and creates multiple bosses to report to. The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Renée Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney, authorizing up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process.
cards.headline: Fort Pierce loses three legal department attorneys as city faces major South Hutchinson Island development decisions
